{{Short description|German mathematical physicist (born 1945)}}

[[File:Hajo Leschke.jpg|thumb|Hajo Leschke in 2023]]
'''Hajo Leschke''' (born 11 February 1945 in [[Wentorf bei Hamburg]]) is a German [[Mathematical physics|mathematical physicist]] and (semi-)retired professor of [[theoretical physics]] at the Friedrich Alexander [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg]] (FAU).{{r|fau}} He is known for rigorous results on model systems in [[Quantum statistical mechanics|quantum (statistical) mechanics]] obtained through [[Functional analysis|functional-analytic]] and [[Probability theory|probabilistic techniques]], jointly with his (former) students and other co-workers. His research topics include: [[Peierls transition|Peierls Transition]], Functional Formulations of Quantum and Stochastic Dynamics, Pekar–Fröhlich [[Polaron]], Quantum [[Spin chain|Spin Chains]], [[Feynman–Kac formula|Feynman–Kac Formulas]], (Random) [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Schrödinger Operators]], Landau-Level Broadening, Lifschitz Tails, [[Anderson localization|Anderson Localization]], Fermionic Entanglement Entropies, Quantum [[Spin glass|Spin Glasses]].

== Academic education ==
Leschke studied physics and mathematics at the [[University of Hamburg]] and graduated with a [[diploma]] in physics (1970) under thesis advisor [[Wolfgang Kundt]] (born 1931). He received his [[doctorate]] in physics (1975) under dissertation advisor [[:de:Uwe Brandt (Physiker)|Uwe Brandt]] (1944–1997) from the [[Technical University of Dortmund]], where he also earned the [[habilitation]] in physics (1981). His studies were supported by the [[Studienstiftung]] des deutschen Volkes (German Academic Scholarship Foundation) and the [[:de:Kurt-Hartwig-Siemers-Wissenschaftspreis|Kurt-Hartwig-Siemers–Wissenschaftspreis]] on the recommendation of [[Werner Döring]] (1911–2006) and of [[Pascual Jordan]]{{r|PJ}} (1902–1980), respectively.{{r|cv}}

== Career ==
Leschke was a research (and teaching) assistant to Ludwig Tewordt (1926–2016) at the University of Hamburg, to Uwe Brandt at the Technical University of Dortmund, to [[Herbert Wagner (physicist)|Herbert Wagner]] (born 1935) at the [[Forschungszentrum Jülich]] (then: KFA Jülich), and to Richard Bausch (born 1935) at the [[Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf]] (HHU) before he became a professor there in 1982 and at FAU in 1983. In 1987, he was a guest professor at the [[University of Georgia]], Athens (UGA) with host [[David P. Landau]] (born 1941). In 2004, he organized the workshop "Mathematics and physics of disordered systems" jointly with Michael Baake, [[:de:Werner Kirsch (Mathematiker)|Werner Kirsch]], and [[Leonid Pastur|Leonid A. Pastur]] at the [[Oberwolfach Research Institute for Mathematics]] (MFO), Germany.{{r|owr}} In 2017, he organized the workshop "Fisher–Hartwig asymptotics, Szegő expansions, and applications to statistical physics" jointly with Alexander V. Sobolev and Wolfgang Spitzer at the American Institute of Mathematics ([[American Institute of Mathematics|AIM]]), then located in San Jose, California.{{r|fha}} From 1998 to 2011, Leschke belonged to the advisory board of the [[Annalen der Physik]]{{r|AdP}}, then edited by Ulrich Eckern (born 1952) at the [[University of Augsburg]].{{r|cv}}

== Notable students ==

Notable doctoral students of Leschke include Peter Müller{{r|pm}} (born 1967) and [[Simone Warzel]] (born 1973). The first one is professor of mathematics at [[LMU Munich]] and [[Dean (education)|dean]] of the Faculty of Mathematics, Informatics, and Statistics (2021–2025). The second one is professor of mathematics at the [[Technical University of Munich]] (TUM) in Garching near Munich.{{r|mgp}}

== Research achievements ==
Leschke's research publications listed below all refer to properties of non-relativistic quantum systems which are modeled by some [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]], that is, by some [[self-adjoint operator]] on [[Hilbert space]] representing the total energy of the system, possibly depending on [[Random variable|random variables]] simulating disorder. In the publications from 2000 to 2017 the Hamiltonian is of [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)#Schrödinger Hamiltonian|Schrödinger type]], that is, an operator for the sum of the kinetic and potential energy of "point-like" particles in [[Euclidean space]]. The two publications with Kurt Broderix (1962–2000) extend previously known continuity properties of the corresponding one-parameter Schrödinger [[C0-semigroup|semigroup]] (or Gibbs operator for different temperatures) to rather general magnetic fields and to (random) potential fields possibly leading to unbounded semigroups; by suitably extending the [[Feynman–Kac formula]] and using the [[diamagnetic inequality]].{{r|LHB}} The other three publications from 2000 to 2004 consider the case of a single particle subject to a constant magnetic field and a [[Random field|random potential field]]. For a Poissonian field with positive single-impurity potential U the low-energy behavior of the integrated (or cumulative) [[density of states]] is derived, depending on the range of U. For a Gaussian random field (without an underlying lattice structure) the first proofs are given for the existence of the density of states and of [[Anderson localization]] in multidimensional continuous space.{{r|CS}}{{r|AW}} The publications in 2014 and 2017 refer to the case of many non-interacting particles which obey [[Fermi–Dirac statistics]]. For the corresponding ideal [[Fermi gas]] in [[Thermodynamic equilibrium|thermodynamic equilibrium]] they contain the first rigorous results on the asymptotic growth of its quantum Rényi [[entropy of entanglement|entropies of (spatial) entanglement]] at arbitrary temperature.{{r|LSS}}{{r|LSS2}} These results have served as a standard of comparison for approximate arguments and/or numerical methods to better understand the correlations in many-fermion systems with interaction.{{r|PL}}{{r|JC}} The publications in 2021 are among the first ones providing rigorous results on quantum versions of the classic(al) [[Spin glass#Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model|Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin-glass model]]. In particular, they prove for the first time the existence of a phase transition (related to [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|spontaneous replica-symmetry breaking]]) if the temperature and the strength of the "transverse" magnetic field are low enough.{{r|LMRW}} The publication in 2023 illuminates this phase transition's relevance to the [[Quantum annealing|quantum-annealing]] algorithm in computer science.{{r|ach}}{{r|vczt}}{{r|kbpsmdd}}
